Hiring software that screens CVs using algorithmic decision-making is now common at large firms. — ALGORITHMIC (adj) = thuộc thuật toán; luôn đứng trước danh từ, ví dụ "algorithmic decision-making". 9. Autonomous cars are designed to make decisions on the road without a person controlling them directly. — AUTONOMOUS (adj) = tự hành; collocation "autonomous vehicles", tránh nhầm với "anonymous". 11. A system that filters news feeds to keep people scrolling is a clear case of reward hacking, optimising engagement while undermining the platform's original purpose. — REWARD HACKING (n) = hiện tượng AI tối ưu chỉ số đo lường thay vì mục tiêu thật; không nhầm với "hacking" xâm nhập máy tính. 12. passages.text: When a 2018 study at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that several widely used facial-analysis systems classified the gender of darker-skinned women with error rates above thirty per cent — compared with under one per cent for lighter-skinned men — the result attracted attention well beyond the technical community. The lead author, Joy Buolamwini, framed the finding not merely as a measurement problem but as a public-policy question: a tool deployed at scale in policing, hiring and border control was producing systematically uneven errors across demographic groups. In the half-decade since, the field of algorithmic fairness has grown into a sizeable research literature, and the disagreements within it now do much of the intellectual work in shaping AI governance proposals worldwide.

The first sustained line of work has focused on what is sometimes called bias measurement. Researchers including Buolamwini and her colleagues at the Algorithmic Justice League have audited commercial systems against carefully curated datasets and reported disparities by skin tone, gender and age. Subsequent audits, conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in the United States, examined nearly two hundred facial-recognition algorithms and found that several mid-tier systems produced false-match rates between ten and a hundred times higher for African-American and East Asian faces than for white faces. The findings are not uniformly negative — top-performing systems substantially closed the gap by 2020 — but the variation across vendors remains, in the institute's careful phrasing, large enough to matter for deployment decisions.

A second tradition, associated with the political theorist Kate Crawford of New York University, has questioned the framing of "bias" itself. In her 2021 book Atlas of AI and a series of related papers, Crawford has argued that focusing on technical disparities tends to narrow public attention to whatever can be measured easily, while leaving the broader structures within which AI is built and deployed largely unexamined. The labour conditions of data annotators, the energy demands of large training runs and the geographies in which automated decisions land most heavily are, in her account, every bit as relevant to fairness as the demographic profile of error rates. The technical audit, she suggests, is necessary but not sufficient.

A third strand has developed inside the formal computer-science literature itself. Researchers at Cornell, including Solon Barocas and his collaborators, have shown that the various mathematical definitions of fairness used in the field — equal false-positive rates across groups, equal predictive value across groups, equal calibration — are typically incompatible with one another except in narrow special cases. The implication, made explicit in a frequently cited 2018 paper, is that no single technical metric can resolve fairness questions on its own; choosing among the metrics involves a value judgement about which kind of error matters more, and to whom. Engineering teams that present a fairness audit as a simple pass-or-fail test, Barocas has cautioned, are obscuring a normative decision rather than escaping it.

These three positions are not in direct opposition, but they pull governance in different directions. If the priority is to reduce measurable disparities in operating systems, the appropriate response is mandatory pre-deployment auditing and continuous post-deployment monitoring. If the priority is to address the wider political economy of AI, the focus shifts to data-collection practices, labour standards and environmental disclosure. If the priority is to recognise trade-offs between fairness metrics, governance has to make room for explicit deliberation about which metric applies in which context.

Comparative work on emerging governance regimes has begun, if not to settle, then at least to clarify these choices. The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force in 2024, classifies systems by risk tier and imposes the strictest requirements on uses such as biometric identification and educational scoring. The United States has so far preferred a sector-by-sector approach, with separate guidance for hiring, healthcare and consumer finance. China has issued specific rules on recommendation algorithms and generative content. None of these regimes, in the view of governance scholars such as Anu Bradford of Columbia Law School, fully reflects any one of the three research positions outlined above. Each represents, instead, a different mixture: heavy in technical audit, light on political economy, partial on metric pluralism.

Defenders of a more flexible approach push back along several lines. Some technologists argue that detailed rules tend to lag the technology and lock in current architectures at the expense of newer entrants. Others note that strict pre-deployment audits can be circumvented by deploying systems in jurisdictions with weaker oversight. None of this disposes of the original concern about uneven errors, but it does suggest that the regulatory trade-offs are sharper than the language of accountability implies.

Call a system "biased" or "unbiased" and the label conceals three separate truths the evidence will not let one merge. Measurable disparities in individual systems are real and have, in several documented cases, shrunk sharply once audited. The wider political economy of AI is real and has, so far, drawn weaker regulatory tools than the technical literature. And the trade-offs between rival mathematical definitions of fairness are real and likely to stay so. The question Buolamwini, Crawford and Barocas keep returning to, each in a different vocabulary, is therefore not whether a system can be made fair in the abstract but who decides which fairness counts.

The practical question is one of timing. Generative systems trained on very large datasets are already raising further fairness questions — consent in training data, uneven access to the most capable models — and governance will go on trailing the technology by a margin set by how fast each of the three research traditions is turned into administrative practice. That margin is rarely short, for a plain reason the past five years make clear: audits, political-economy analyses and metric debates seldom arrive at the regulatory desk in the same week, and a rule cannot act on findings it has not yet received.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our computer-science-ethics series — focusing on the empirical literature concerning algorithmic bias and fairness audit methodology in deployed classification systems. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Joaquin Berriozabal — that's B-E-R-R-I-O-Z-A-B-A-L, no hyphen, double-R only. Berriozabal's 2017 monograph reframed algorithmic fairness from a binary equal-treatment standard into what he calls "stratified parity theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The benchmark audit corpus I'll reference today was first compiled in 2015 — sorry, let me correct that, 2014; the published descriptive statistics in 2015 covered data collected in 2014. So whenever I refer to the baseline year, please record 2014. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Berriozabal's framework USED TO be operationalised using single-axis demographic-parity tests, NOW the field deploys multi-axis intersectional audits incorporating counterfactual probes, and from 2027 a multi-institution consortium WILL be rolling out continuous-monitoring modules. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, multi-axis intersectional audits. Moving to terminology. The fairness concept Berriozabal foregrounds — the systematic differential in classifier accuracy across population subgroups attributable to training-data composition — is termed "representational harm". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: data skew, sampling bias, distributional drift. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Berriozabal's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is representational harm — r-e-p-r-e-s-e-n-t-a-t-i-o-n-a-l harm. So when the older literature uses data skew or sampling bias, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what computer scientists call the "fairness criteria taxonomy". When auditors describe how a classifier's outputs satisfy or violate fairness constraints, they sketch a graded taxonomy running from demographic parity through equalised odds to calibration within groups. So, you know, you'll see auditors who only check whether positive prediction rates match across subgroups — that's demographic parity. Or auditors who additionally check error-rate symmetry across the same subgroups — that's equalised odds. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the umbrella term. The umbrella term is the fairness criteria taxonomy. [pause:3s] Now, the audit data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the eighty-four deployed classifiers we audited across the public sector last year, MOST showed measurable subgroup disparities — roughly sixty-eight per cent. Only a few — about nine per cent — passed every fairness threshold, and some — twenty-three per cent — showed disparities only on one criterion but not others. So measurable disparity dominates numerically, though the fully-passing tail, though small, demonstrates that compliance is achievable. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "feedback-loop amplification". This refers to the dynamic in which a deployed model's predictions reshape the data it subsequently observes, magnifying initial disparities over successive retraining cycles. At the Riverside Municipal Hiring Platform, our auditors documented sixty-one observable amplification episodes across one calendar year. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that larger training corpora linearly reduce subgroup disparities is, frankly, not supported. Most of the classifiers in our audit did NOT exhibit the predicted monotonic reduction in disparity as training-data volume increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a plateau curve, with no further fairness gain beyond a threshold of around ten million labelled examples. So the older "more-data-fixes-bias" hypothesis, which predicts linear improvement, is empirically NOT corroborated by our audit data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT multi-axis intersectional state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in today's seminar this afternoon. I want you to focus on the counterfactual probe protocols specifically, not the continuous-monitoring futures or the legacy single-axis demographic-parity instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: algorithmic fairness is a multi-axis property, not a binary equal-treatment standard; the technical term for subgroup accuracy differential is representational harm; measurable disparity dominates at roughly sixty-eight per cent; and the more-data-fixes-bias hypothesis is empirically not supported. Next week we'll examine governance and audit-reporting architectures. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

band_comparison.text: Bài Band 8 nâng phần Overview thành một nhận định xuyên suốt cả hai bảng số liệu — chỉ ra rằng vốn đầu tư và mức độ tích hợp AI "chỉ gắn kết lỏng lẻo" (loosely coupled) — trong khi bài Band 7 chỉ nêu các cực trị của từng bảng riêng lẻ mà chưa kết nối chúng lại. Về từ vựng, Band 8 sử dụng lớp từ và danh hóa (nominalisation) tinh tế hơn hẳn, như "capital outlay", "sectoral uptake", "capital intensity", "languished", "partially inverts this picture", đồng thời vận dụng cấu trúc câu chẻ (cleft sentence) "What the comparison reveals is that…" để nhấn mạnh luận điểm kết luận. Ngoài ra, Band 8 diễn giải sâu hơn về nguyên nhân đằng sau độ lệch giữa đầu tư và mức áp dụng — như chu kỳ mua sắm (procurement cycles) và sự thận trọng về quy định (regulatory caution) — thay vì chỉ dừng lại ở việc mô tả số liệu như Band 7, nhờ đó nâng rõ rệt tiêu chí Task Achievement và Coherence and Cohesion.

blocks.text: The two bar charts compare five global sectors — Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing, Retail and Defence — in terms of the volume of AI deployment investment and the corresponding enterprise adoption rate in 2024.

Overall, finance emerged as the clear frontrunner on both measures, while the adoption ranking broadly mirrors the investment ranking without matching it exactly. Notably, defence funded AI heavily yet recorded the lowest uptake of all five sectors.

Turning first to investment, finance attracted by far the largest inflow, at US$56bn, followed by defence at US$44bn and healthcare at US$38bn. Manufacturing and retail commanded the smallest budgets, at US$32bn and US$28bn respectively.

The adoption panel tells a partly different story. Financial firms again led the field, with 78% of large companies running at least one AI system, whereas defence trailed at 52% despite comparable funding. Healthcare and manufacturing converged in the low-60s, at 58% and 64%, while retail reached 62%. The figures suggest that capital and integration tend to advance together, yet defence under-adopts relative to its budget, implying that funding alone does not guarantee operational integration.
The two bar charts compare AI deployment investment and enterprise adoption across five global sectors — Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing, Retail and Defence — in 2024.

Overall, finance stands out as the unambiguous frontrunner on both metrics, and although the adoption hierarchy broadly echoes the investment hierarchy, the two do not move in lockstep. Most strikingly, defence pairs heavy capital outlay with the weakest sectoral uptake, suggesting that money and integration are only loosely coupled.

In terms of expenditure, the financial sector attracted by far the largest inflow, at US$56bn, comfortably ahead of defence (US$44bn) and healthcare (US$38bn). Manufacturing and retail occupied the bottom of the field, commanding US$32bn and US$28bn respectively.

The adoption panel partially inverts this picture. While financial firms again topped the ranking, with 78% running AI in production, defence languished at 52% despite a comparable budget — the poorest return on investment of any sector. Healthcare, manufacturing and retail clustered closely in the low-60s, at 58%, 64% and 62%. What the comparison reveals is that capital intensity does not reliably translate into operational adoption: procurement cycles and regulatory caution, rather than funding, appear to govern how far AI is actually embedded.

blocks.text: By taking over gruelling, high-risk operations such as deep-sea welding or bomb disposal, large-scale automation removes human beings from environments where a single error could prove fatal.
Machine learning systems can augment human capabilities by processing vast datasets at a speed and scale that no team of analysts could ever replicate.

Intelligent tutoring systems hold out the promise of genuinely personalised, scalable education, adapting instantly to an individual learner's pace rather than forcing every student through an identical curriculum.
Repetitive, mundane administrative work — data entry, invoice processing, basic scheduling — can be delegated to software, freeing employees to focus on tasks that demand judgement and creativity.
Where historical records contain entrenched prejudices, algorithmic bias can quietly perpetuate, and even amplify, discrimination in hiring, lending and policing decisions.
The proliferation of deepfakes makes it trivially easy for malicious actors to fabricate convincing footage, eroding public trust in genuine video and audio evidence.
Widespread deployment of facial recognition and other monitoring tools has normalised a level of mass surveillance that would have seemed dystopian a generation ago.
Heavy reliance on automated systems can leave organisations dangerously exposed whenever those systems fail, since employees may no longer retain the manual skills needed to step in.
Relentless competitive pressure pushes firms to adopt state-of-the-art technology simply to avoid being undercut by rivals who have already automated their operations.
The exponential growth in computing power and the availability of enormous training datasets have allowed frontier models to advance far more rapidly than most experts anticipated.
Falling costs of sensors, robotics and cloud computing have made labour-saving technology affordable even for small and medium-sized enterprises, not just industrial giants.
A chronic shortage of skilled labour in certain sectors has driven employers to seek autonomous alternatives capable of operating around the clock without fatigue.
Sustained automation gradually reshapes entire industries, rendering whole categories of routine clerical and manufacturing roles redundant within a single generation.
As algorithms mediate ever more decisions, an accountability gap emerges: victims of a flawed automated decision often cannot identify who, if anyone, should be held responsible.
Job displacement among blue-collar and clerical workers tends to widen the gap between those with in-demand technical skills and those without.
The normalisation of AI-driven content moderation and recommendation has subtly altered public discourse, occasionally amplifying sensational material at the expense of nuanced debate.
Regulators face a persistent challenge in keeping pace with frontier models, since legislation is typically drafted years after the technology it seeks to govern has already matured.
Detecting a well-crafted deepfake is becoming increasingly difficult even for trained specialists, let alone ordinary members of the public scrolling through social media.
Retraining a displaced workforce is far harder than it sounds, since reskilling programmes must contend with workers whose entire careers were built around now-obsolete manual skills.

The tendency of some optimisation systems to engage in reward hacking — satisfying the letter of a target metric while betraying its underlying purpose — makes AI behaviour difficult to predict reliably.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: Mandating algorithmic transparency for high-stakes applications would allow independent auditors to examine how automated decisions are reached before they are deployed at scale.
Governments could fund large-scale reskilling initiatives so that workers whose roles have become redundant can transition into occupations that automation is unlikely to threaten soon.
Subjecting frontier models to rigorous, pre-deployment safety evaluations, comparable to those required of new pharmaceuticals, would help close the current accountability gap.
A calibrated regulation regime — neither reflexively banning innovation nor leaving it entirely unchecked — could curb the worst abuses of mass surveillance while preserving genuine benefits.
Many technologists remain convinced that AI is fundamentally a double-edged sword: capable of astonishing good, yet equally capable of grave harm if left unchecked.
A vocal contingent regards automation as an unambiguous game changer, one that will eventually eliminate poverty by making goods and services radically cheaper to produce.
Sceptics counter that public debate around a potential technological singularity distracts from the more mundane, near-term harms already being caused by narrow AI systems.
There is widespread agreement that AI's rapid diffusion has opened a can of worms concerning privacy, intellectual property and the very definition of authentic human work.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: Developers of frontier models bear a heightened duty to invest in AI alignment research, ensuring that increasingly capable systems remain answerable to human oversight.
Governments carry the primary responsibility for closing the accountability gap through legislation that clearly assigns liability whenever an autonomous system causes harm.
Employers who adopt large-scale automation have an obligation to support the workers they displace, rather than treating redundancy purely as a cost-saving measure.
Individual users also share some responsibility, since a more discerning public that critically evaluates AI-generated content would blunt the impact of deepfakes and misinformation.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: Although critics warn of mass unemployment, proponents note that automation has historically augmented rather than eliminated human labour, giving rise to entirely new professions.
While fears of algorithmic bias are legitimate, defenders argue that a well-audited algorithm can, in principle, be far more consistent and less prejudiced than a fallible human decision-maker.
Sceptics of existential-risk rhetoric contend that current systems remain narrow and lack genuine intent, so sentient, self-directed machines are a far more distant prospect than headlines suggest.

It could be argued that abandoning promising research over speculative, worst-case scenarios is both economically costly and difficult to justify when set against tangible gains such as faster medical diagnostics.
A growing body of research suggests that autonomous vehicles will become significantly more common on public roads over the coming decade, gradually reshaping urban transport and logistics.
As frontier models grow more capable, debate is likely to intensify over whether society is approaching a genuine technological singularity or merely incremental, if impressive, progress.
Intelligent tutoring systems are expected to become embedded in mainstream education, supplementing rather than replacing human teachers in the foreseeable future.

Pressure from civil society and international bodies is likely to push more governments toward calibrated regulation, mandating algorithmic transparency for any system used in high-stakes decision-making.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas earlier waves of automation mainly displaced manual, blue-collar labour, today's algorithmic systems increasingly threaten white-collar and even creative occupations once thought immune.
Unlike traditional software, which merely follows fixed rules, machine learning systems can adapt and improve their own performance, making their long-term behaviour considerably harder to predict.
Compared with earlier, narrow applications of AI, frontier models demonstrate a far broader range of competencies, blurring the line between specialised tools and general-purpose intelligence.
In contrast to conventional surveillance, which relied on human operators reviewing footage, AI-powered facial recognition enables mass surveillance at a scale and cost previously unimaginable.
A hypothetical case study contrasting a factory before and after adopting large-scale automation could illustrate both productivity gains and the resulting job displacement.
Reports from technology-policy think tanks that document instances of algorithmic bias in hiring or lending software offer concrete evidence of the risks discussed above.
Journalistic investigations into the spread of political deepfakes provide vivid, real-world illustrations of how synthetic media can undermine public trust.
Comparative national statistics on reskilling programme uptake could be cited to show how different governments are responding to workforce displacement at varying speeds.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Few technologies have generated as much utopian enthusiasm and apocalyptic fear as artificial intelligence. While some commentators warn that AI poses existential risks capable of overshadowing every conceivable benefit, others insist that such alarmism is overblown. I largely disagree with the strong existential claim, but accept that significant near-term risks demand serious regulation.

Those who fear AI tend to point to its breakneck pace of development. It is precisely the speed at which large models are scaling that worries researchers, since algorithmic systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains — lending, hiring, policing — before alignment problems have been solved. Furthermore, autonomous weapons, deepfakes and mass surveillance show how the technology can be weaponised, while automation may render entire occupations redundant.

On the other hand, those who push back on existential framing note, not unreasonably, that current AI systems operate strictly within human-defined objectives and training data. They lack consciousness and any genuine intent; their failure modes, while serious, are essentially engineering problems. Moreover, AI has already delivered tangible benefits — earlier cancer detection, accelerated drug discovery, personalised tutoring — that would be reckless to forfeit on the basis of speculative scenarios.

In my view, the existential framing is largely premature, but the precautionary impulse it expresses is legitimate. Provided that governments invest in alignment research, mandate algorithmic transparency and update labour and liability law, the benefits of AI can be harnessed while the genuine risks are kept under control. Outright pessimism, however, risks ceding the technology's development to actors far less interested in safety.

Few technological frontiers have polarised expert opinion as sharply as artificial intelligence. While prominent researchers warn that frontier systems pose existential risks capable of eclipsing every benefit, others contend that such framing is premature and counterproductive. My own position is that, on present evidence, the strong existential claim is overstated, although the near-term risks of unaligned AI plainly justify aggressive regulation.

Proponents of the existential thesis emphasise the trajectory rather than the present capability of frontier models. So rapid has progress in deep learning become that AI alignment — the project of ensuring that increasingly autonomous systems pursue human-compatible objectives — lags conspicuously behind capability research. Were a sufficiently general system deployed without robust alignment, the consequences could plausibly be irreversible. Furthermore, even sub-superintelligent AI already enables algorithmic bias, mass surveillance, autonomous weapons and deepfake-mediated destabilisation, none of which require sentience to do considerable harm.

By contrast, sceptics of the apocalyptic register argue that contemporary AI remains narrow, brittle and devoid of intent. Its failure modes, while non-trivial, reflect engineering and governance gaps rather than the harbingers of a singularity. Set against the speculative downside is a substantial and accumulating upside: AI-assisted radiology now matches expert clinicians in several diagnostic domains, machine-learning models accelerate drug discovery, and intelligent tutoring systems promise scalable, personalised education. To suspend such applications on speculative grounds would be both costly and ethically questionable.

In my view, the most defensible posture is calibrated rather than apocalyptic. Provided that states mandate algorithmic transparency, fund alignment research and update labour, liability and competition law, the substantial benefits of AI can be realised while existential pathways are deliberately closed off. Pessimism untethered from policy merely concedes the field to less cautious developers.

PHẦN A: 1. A well-defined algorithm tells the computer exactly how to sort the data. — ALGORITHM (n) = thuật toán, chuỗi bước xử lý dữ liệu có quy tắc rõ ràng; collocation "a complex/well-defined algorithm". 2. Factories are increasingly relying on automation to carry out tasks that used to require manual labour. — AUTOMATION (n, không đếm được) = tự động hoá; collocation "large-scale/workplace automation". 3. Many economists worry about job displacement as software takes over routine paperwork. — DISPLACEMENT (n) = sự mất việc do máy móc/công nghệ thay thế; collocation cố định "job displacement", không nói "job replacement". 4. Some data-entry clerks are being made redundant because their jobs are no longer necessary. — REDUNDANT (adj) = dư thừa, mất việc; cấu trúc "make sb redundant" (Anh-Anh). 5. Sorting emails all day can feel mundane and repetitive for an office worker. — MUNDANE (adj) = tẻ nhạt, lặp đi lặp lại; collocation "mundane tasks/routine". 6. Many citizens are uneasy about the level of surveillance that cameras and software enable in public. — SURVEILLANCE (n) = sự giám sát; collocation "mass surveillance", chính tả có hai chữ "l". 7. Some datasets contain bias that unfairly favours one group over another, which can make automated decisions unfair. — BIAS (n) = thiên kiến, thiên lệch; collocation "algorithmic/gender bias". 8. Hiring software that screens CVs using algorithmic decision-making is now common at large firms. — ALGORITHMIC (adj) = thuộc thuật toán; luôn đứng trước danh từ, ví dụ "algorithmic decision-making". 9. Digital assistants can augment what a person can do, handling huge amounts of information almost instantly. — AUGMENT (v) = bổ trợ, tăng cường; collocation "augment human capabilities", tránh nhầm với "argument". 10. Autonomous cars are designed to make decisions on the road without a person controlling them directly. — AUTONOMOUS (adj) = tự hành; collocation "autonomous vehicles", tránh nhầm với "anonymous". 11. A system that filters news feeds to keep people scrolling is a clear case of reward hacking, optimising engagement while undermining the platform's original purpose. — REWARD HACKING (n) = hiện tượng AI tối ưu chỉ số đo lường thay vì mục tiêu thật; không nhầm với "hacking" xâm nhập máy tính. 12. Deepfakes created with AI can make it look as though someone said something they never actually said. — DEEPFAKE (n) = video/hình ảnh giả mạo bằng AI; viết liền một từ.

The Displacement Effect: The World Economic Forum estimates that AI will displace 85 million jobs globally by 2025, particularly in data entry, accounting, and basic customer service.

The Rise of Deepfakes: The malicious use of AI to generate hyper-realistic fake videos is becoming a major threat to political stability and individual reputation, forcing platforms to develop counter-AI detection tools.

2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: AI and Employment (Utopia vs. Mass Unemployment)

Utopia (Pros): Automation eliminates menial, repetitive, and highly dangerous tasks (e.g., bomb defusal, deep-sea welding); it drastically boosts industrial productivity; new sophisticated roles will emerge requiring emotional intelligence and creativity.

Mass Unemployment (Cons): Blue-collar workers face severe displacement and risk becoming entirely redundant; the speed of automation is outpacing the government's ability to provide effective reskilling programmes.
Topic: Big Data & Privacy Concerns
Benefits: Companies analyse big data to accurately predict consumer behaviour, offering highly personalized services and optimising supply chains.

Drawbacks: The collection of vast amounts of personal data without explicit consent opens a can of worms regarding privacy; facial recognition is increasingly used for unauthorized mass surveillance by authoritative regimes.
Topic: The Singularity (Should we fear super-intelligent AI?)

Arguments FOR fear: If machines become fully sentient and surpass human cognitive abilities, they may view humanity as an obstacle or threat; algorithmic bias could lead to dystopian societal control.

Arguments AGAINST fear: AI strictly operates within the boundaries of human programming and mathematical algorithms; it lacks true consciousness, intuition, and empathy; the focus should be on proper regulation, not sci-fi paranoia.

Cue card: Describe a way AI has affected your daily life. You should say: what the AI tool or service is; how often you use it; what you use it for; and explain how it has changed your routine or habits.
Model Answer (≈ 272 words, Band 7.5–8.0):

The AI tool that has most palpably reshaped my daily routine is ChatGPT — and specifically the GPT-4 class of large language models that became broadly accessible in late 2022. What I find genuinely transformative about this technology is not any single capability in isolation, but the way it has compressed cognitive workflows that previously consumed hours into matters of minutes.

I use it on a near-daily basis — probably four or five times a day on weekdays. My usage spans a fairly wide spectrum: drafting professional correspondence, summarising dense academic papers on bioethics for my research, debugging Python scripts when my data-analysis pipeline misbehaves, and increasingly, using it as a Socratic interlocutor to stress-test arguments I'm developing. What I've consciously avoided is outsourcing my actual thinking; I treat it more as a sparring partner than a ghostwriter.

The impact on my routine has been, frankly, profound. Tasks that previously required several rounds of revision now reach a publishable first draft in a single sitting. According to research I came across recently, knowledge workers using generative AI saw meaningful productivity gains on writing tasks. That tracks with my own experience.

That said, I'm acutely conscious of the trade-offs. Algorithmic hallucination — the tendency of these models to confabulate plausible-sounding falsehoods — means I've had to develop almost paranoid verification habits. There's also a creeping concern about cognitive offloading: skills atrophy when you stop exercising them. So while AI has indisputably accelerated my output, I've come to view it as a Faustian bargain of sorts. The productivity gains are real and substantial, but maintaining intellectual hygiene around AI alignment and source verification is, I think, non-negotiable.

sections.title: PART 2 — Describe a way AI has affected your daily life

blocks.text: Q1: Should AI development be slowed down to allow regulation to catch up?

I'd argue for a calibrated slowdown rather than a blanket moratorium, which I think is both impractical and counterproductive. The 2023 open letter signed by Yoshua Bengio and others calling for a six-month pause was, in retrospect, more a rhetorical intervention than a feasible policy. What I do think is essential is regulatory parity — frontier AI labs should be subject to pre-deployment safety evaluations comparable to those required for pharmaceuticals or nuclear materials. The EU AI Act, which came into force in 2024, represents a credible attempt at risk-tiered governance, banning unacceptable-risk applications like social scoring while permitting innovation in low-risk domains. The deeper issue, though, is the unsolved AI alignment problem: we genuinely don't know how to ensure that increasingly capable systems will reliably pursue human-compatible objectives. Until that's resolved, deploying frontier models at scale strikes me as recklessly premature.
Q2: Can AI ever be truly creative, or is it merely imitative?

This hinges entirely on how one defines creativity, and I'd venture a nuanced position. If creativity means novel recombination of existing elements, then large language models and diffusion models like Midjourney are demonstrably creative — they produce outputs no human ever explicitly composed. However, if we adopt a stricter definition involving intentionality, lived experience and aesthetic agency, then current AI falls decisively short. These systems lack what philosophers call qualia — the subjective texture of experience that, arguably, animates genuine artistic expression. What's more, they are fundamentally derivative: trained on vast corpora of human-generated content, they essentially remix the statistical patterns of their training data. So in my view, AI is a sophisticated creative collaborator rather than an autonomous creator. Whether that distinction survives the advent of artificial general intelligence is, of course, an open question.
Q3: Will AI eventually replace human judgement in high-stakes domains?

In narrow technical domains, it already is — and largely for the better. AI radiologists now outperform their human counterparts on certain cancer-detection tasks; AlphaFold has revolutionised protein structure prediction. What I'm far more sceptical about is replacing human judgement in domains involving moral reasoning, contextual nuance or accountability. Take judicial sentencing: predictive risk-assessment tools like COMPAS have been shown to encode racial bias, illustrating that algorithmic governance can launder historical prejudice under a veneer of objectivity. The fundamental issue is that AI systems optimise for measurable proxies, whereas human judgement integrates tacit knowledge, ethical intuition and democratic legitimacy. So my view is that AI should function as an augmentation layer — surfacing patterns, flagging anomalies, modelling counterfactuals — while final accountability remains squarely with humans. The hybrid model, I think, is both more accurate and more ethically defensible.
T21 — ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
Lecture title: "AI Alignment, Generative-Model Ethics and the Algorithmic-Bias Problem"
1. Section Type

2. Pre-Listening Vocabulary (4–5 words)

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas (before listening)

Generative AI ethics may be reframed around provenance, consent and harm.
Algorithmic bias will likely be presented as inherited from training data, not invented by models.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good morning. Today's lecture interrogates three pressing problems in contemporary AI ethics: AI alignment, the ethics of generative AI and the algorithmic-bias problem. The reassuring framing of these models as neutral tools, I will argue, collapses on inspection.

> Consider, first, AI alignment. The Berkeley computer scientist Stuart Russell has argued that the canonical AI design — give the machine a fixed objective and let it optimise — is provably unsafe at scale. A system told to maximise paperclip production, in the philosopher Nick Bostrom's famous thought experiment, may convert the planet's atoms into paperclips. More mundanely, recommender systems told to maximise engagement have reward-hacked their way into amplifying outrage. Aligning frontier models with plural human values remains technically open.

> Now, generative AI ethics. Models such as GPT-4, Claude and Stable Diffusion are trained on scraped corpora of unprecedented scale — the LAION-5B dataset alone contains five point eight billion image-text pairs. Three ethical fault lines emerge: provenance — was the training data lawfully acquired; consent — did authors and artists agree; and downstream harm — deepfakes, non-consensual imagery and synthetic disinformation. The European Union's AI Act of 2024 imposes tiered obligations on general-purpose AI providers.

> Finally, algorithmic bias. The computer scientist Joy Buolamwini's 2018 Gender Shades audit found that commercial facial-recognition systems misclassified darker-skinned women at error rates exceeding thirty-four percent, against under one percent for lighter-skinned men. Bias, it transpires, is rarely invented by the model; it is inherited from the training distribution and the labelling pipeline. Fairness, therefore, demands upstream auditing, not merely cosmetic post-hoc correction.

Before we read too much triumph into that curve, let me complicate the picture with a phenomenon the alignment literature has only recently begun to name properly: emergent capability. Researchers at Anthropic and elsewhere have documented that certain abilities — chain-of-step arithmetic, say, or rudimentary deception in evaluation settings — simply do not exist below a parameter threshold and then, um, appear almost discontinuously once you cross it. The unsettling corollary is that a model can pass every safety test we devise at one scale and acquire an untested, unanticipated competence at the next. [pause] So the very thing that makes these systems commercially thrilling — their unpredictability under scaling — is precisely what makes them governance-resistant.

Let me pivot to a sharper case on the bias front, because I worry the Gender Shades story can be misread as a solved problem. It isn't. Consider clinical algorithms. A widely cited 2019 study in Science examined a risk-prediction tool used on roughly two hundred million Americans and found it systematically under-referred Black patients to high-need care programmes — not because race was an input, mind you, but because the model used prior healthcare spending as a proxy for need. And since less had historically been spent on Black patients, the proxy laundered structural inequity into an apparently objective score. Well, that is the crucial subtlety: bias migrates. Scrub it from one variable and it reappears, wearing the respectable clothing of a correlated feature.

There's a counter-argument I should fairly represent. Some engineers contend that these are transient, early-deployment failures — that with richer data and better proxies, fairness is asymptotically achievable. [pause] I'm sceptical, and here's why. The choice of what to optimise for — engagement, spending, conviction rates — is itself a value judgement smuggled in as a technical specification. No quantity of clean data resolves a question that is, at bottom, normative rather than statistical. Which raises the obvious question of who, exactly, should be empowered to make that judgement, and under what democratic mandate — and that, naturally, returns us to the regulatory terrain…
> The synthesis is sobering: AI ethics is not a deliverable but a discipline. Now, turning to figure six, which plots model scale against bias-mitigation efficacy…

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~179 từ)

The two bar charts compare five global sectors — Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing, Retail and Defence — in terms of the volume of AI deployment investment and the corresponding enterprise adoption rate in 2024.

Overall, finance emerged as the clear frontrunner on both measures, while the adoption ranking broadly mirrors the investment ranking without matching it exactly. Notably, defence funded AI heavily yet recorded the lowest uptake of all five sectors.

Turning first to investment, finance attracted by far the largest inflow, at US$56bn, followed by defence at US$44bn and healthcare at US$38bn. Manufacturing and retail commanded the smallest budgets, at US$32bn and US$28bn respectively.

The adoption panel tells a partly different story. Financial firms again led the field, with 78% of large companies running at least one AI system, whereas defence trailed at 52% despite comparable funding. Healthcare and manufacturing converged in the low-60s, at 58% and 64%, while retail reached 62%. The figures suggest that capital and integration tend to advance together, yet defence under-adopts relative to its budget, implying that funding alone does not guarantee operational integration.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~194 từ)
The two bar charts compare AI deployment investment and enterprise adoption across five global sectors — Healthcare, Finance, Manufacturing, Retail and Defence — in 2024.

Overall, finance stands out as the unambiguous frontrunner on both metrics, and although the adoption hierarchy broadly echoes the investment hierarchy, the two do not move in lockstep. Most strikingly, defence pairs heavy capital outlay with the weakest sectoral uptake, suggesting that money and integration are only loosely coupled.

In terms of expenditure, the financial sector attracted by far the largest inflow, at US$56bn, comfortably ahead of defence (US$44bn) and healthcare (US$38bn). Manufacturing and retail occupied the bottom of the field, commanding US$32bn and US$28bn respectively.

The adoption panel partially inverts this picture. While financial firms again topped the ranking, with 78% running AI in production, defence languished at 52% despite a comparable budget — the poorest return on investment of any sector. Healthcare, manufacturing and retail clustered closely in the low-60s, at 58%, 64% and 62%. What the comparison reveals is that capital intensity does not reliably translate into operational adoption: procurement cycles and regulatory caution, rather than funding, appear to govern how far AI is actually embedded.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~255 words)

Few technologies have generated as much utopian enthusiasm and apocalyptic fear as artificial intelligence. While some commentators warn that AI poses existential risks capable of overshadowing every conceivable benefit, others insist that such alarmism is overblown. I largely disagree with the strong existential claim, but accept that significant near-term risks demand serious regulation.

Those who fear AI tend to point to its breakneck pace of development. It is precisely the speed at which large models are scaling that worries researchers, since algorithmic systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains — lending, hiring, policing — before alignment problems have been solved. Furthermore, autonomous weapons, deepfakes and mass surveillance show how the technology can be weaponised, while automation may render entire occupations redundant.

On the other hand, those who push back on existential framing note, not unreasonably, that current AI systems operate strictly within human-defined objectives and training data. They lack consciousness and any genuine intent; their failure modes, while serious, are essentially engineering problems. Moreover, AI has already delivered tangible benefits — earlier cancer detection, accelerated drug discovery, personalised tutoring — that would be reckless to forfeit on the basis of speculative scenarios.

In my view, the existential framing is largely premature, but the precautionary impulse it expresses is legitimate. Provided that governments invest in alignment research, mandate algorithmic transparency and update labour and liability law, the benefits of AI can be harnessed while the genuine risks are kept under control. Outright pessimism, however, risks ceding the technology's development to actors far less interested in safety.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~283 words)

Few technological frontiers have polarised expert opinion as sharply as artificial intelligence. While prominent researchers warn that frontier systems pose existential risks capable of eclipsing every benefit, others contend that such framing is premature and counterproductive. My own position is that, on present evidence, the strong existential claim is overstated, although the near-term risks of unaligned AI plainly justify aggressive regulation.

Proponents of the existential thesis emphasise the trajectory rather than the present capability of frontier models. So rapid has progress in deep learning become that AI alignment — the project of ensuring that increasingly autonomous systems pursue human-compatible objectives — lags conspicuously behind capability research. Were a sufficiently general system deployed without robust alignment, the consequences could plausibly be irreversible. Furthermore, even sub-superintelligent AI already enables algorithmic bias, mass surveillance, autonomous weapons and deepfake-mediated destabilisation, none of which require sentience to do considerable harm.

By contrast, sceptics of the apocalyptic register argue that contemporary AI remains narrow, brittle and devoid of intent. Its failure modes, while non-trivial, reflect engineering and governance gaps rather than the harbingers of a singularity. Set against the speculative downside is a substantial and accumulating upside: AI-assisted radiology now matches expert clinicians in several diagnostic domains, machine-learning models accelerate drug discovery, and intelligent tutoring systems promise scalable, personalised education. To suspend such applications on speculative grounds would be both costly and ethically questionable.

In my view, the most defensible posture is calibrated rather than apocalyptic. Provided that states mandate algorithmic transparency, fund alignment research and update labour, liability and competition law, the substantial benefits of AI can be realised while existential pathways are deliberately closed off. Pessimism untethered from policy merely concedes the field to less cautious developers.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dung cau truc cao cap day dac (dao ngu 'So rapid has progress... become that...', dao ngu dieu kien 'Were a sufficiently general system deployed...', dao ngu 'Set against the speculative downside is...') trong khi Band 7 chi dung cleft mot lan.

•  Band 8 thay cum hoi journalese cua Band 7 ('breakneck pace', 'reckless to forfeit', 'machine takeover') bang lexis Band 8 chinh xac ('frontier models', 'sub-superintelligent', 'deepfake-mediated destabilisation', 'a singularity', 'calibrated').
•  Band 8 co lap truong dinh luong sac hon ('on present evidence', 'calibrated rather than apocalyptic') va cohesion mach lac hon, nang Task Response va Lexical Resource len mot bac so voi Band 7.

vocabulary.common_error: Cấu trúc phổ biến là 'make sb redundant' (Anh-Anh, nghĩa sa thải), khác với 'fire sb' vốn mang hàm ý kỷ luật.
vocabulary.definition_en: no longer needed or useful; (of an employee) dismissed because a job is no longer necessary
vocabulary.definition_vi: dư thừa, mất việc (do không còn cần thiết)
vocabulary.example: Many office clerks are being made redundant as automation takes over administrative work.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'redundant' nghe giống 'refund' → công ty 'hoàn trả' lại vị trí vì không còn cần.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tẻ nhạt, tầm thường, lặp đi lặp lại, thiếu hứng thú.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Automation promises to skyrocket productivity by handling repetitive and **mundane** tasks.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"mundane" gần "Monday" (thứ Hai) → công việc tẻ nhạt lặp lại mỗi tuần.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'mundane' (tẻ nhạt) với 'mundane' trong nghĩa cổ 'thuộc về trần thế' — trong IELTS chỉ dùng nghĩa 'nhàm chán'.
vocabulary.definition_en: lacking interest or excitement; dull and routine
vocabulary.definition_vi: tẻ nhạt, tầm thường, lặp đi lặp lại
vocabulary.example: Automation promises to skyrocket productivity by handling repetitive and mundane tasks.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'mundane' gần 'Monday' (thứ Hai) → công việc tẻ nhạt lặp lại mỗi tuần.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự giám sát, theo dõi, đặc biệt bằng công nghệ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Facial recognition systems raise severe fears of mass **surveillance** and the loss of privacy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Pháp "sur-" (trên) + "veiller" (canh gác) → quan sát từ trên xuống, theo dõi sát sao.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả dễ sai: 'surveillance' có hai chữ 'l' và kết thúc bằng '-ance', không phải '-ence'.
vocabulary.definition_en: close observation of a person or group, especially one suspected of wrongdoing, or mass monitoring of populations
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự giám sát, theo dõi (đặc biệt bằng công nghệ)
vocabulary.example: Facial recognition systems raise severe fears of mass surveillance and the loss of privacy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Pháp 'sur-' (trên) + 'veiller' (canh gác) → quan sát từ trên xuống, theo dõi sát sao.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Điểm kỳ dị công nghệ, thời điểm AI vượt trí tuệ con người và không thể kiểm soát.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> As we move closer to a theoretical point known as the **singularity**, society must navigate these challenges carefully.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"singular" (duy nhất, đặc biệt) → điểm mốc duy nhất, không thể quay lại, khi máy móc vượt con người.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong ngữ cảnh AI luôn có mạo từ xác định: 'the singularity', không nói 'a singularity' trừ khi dùng nghĩa toán học khác.
vocabulary.definition_en: the hypothetical future point at which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible, resulting in superintelligent AI
vocabulary.definition_vi: điểm kỳ dị công nghệ (thời điểm AI vượt trí tuệ con người)
vocabulary.example: As we move closer to a theoretical point known as the singularity, society must navigate these challenges carefully.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'singular' (duy nhất, đặc biệt) → điểm mốc duy nhất, không thể quay lại, khi máy móc vượt con người.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thiên kiến, thiên lệch trong dữ liệu hoặc quyết định.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Algorithmic **bias** can perpetuate, and even amplify, existing social inequalities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"bias" nghe như "by us" → góc nhìn nghiêng về "phía chúng ta", không khách quan.
vocabulary.common_error: Động từ dạng quá khứ là 'biased' (một chữ 's'), không phải 'biassed'; đừng nhầm 'bias' (thiên kiến) với 'basis' (nền tảng).
vocabulary.definition_en: prejudice in favour of or against one thing, person, or group compared with another, often in an unfair way; systematic error in data
vocabulary.definition_vi: thiên kiến, thiên lệch (trong dữ liệu hoặc quyết định)
vocabulary.example: Algorithmic bias can perpetuate, and even amplify, existing social inequalities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'bias' nghe như 'by us' → góc nhìn nghiêng về 'phía chúng ta', không khách quan.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc thuật toán, mang tính hệ thống hoá bằng máy tính.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Algorithmic** decision-making is now used to screen job applications at many large companies.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"algorithm" + "-ic" → tính từ mô tả bất cứ điều gì vận hành theo thuật toán.
vocabulary.common_error: Là tính từ nên phải đứng trước danh từ ('algorithmic bias'), không dùng thay cho danh từ 'algorithm'.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to or carried out by a set of computational rules or steps, especially in computing
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc thuật toán, mang tính hệ thống hoá bằng máy tính
vocabulary.example: Algorithmic decision-making is now used to screen job applications at many large companies.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'algorithm' + '-ic' → tính từ mô tả bất cứ điều gì vận hành theo thuật toán.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bổ trợ, tăng cường bằng cách thêm vào cái đã có.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Artificial intelligence can **augment** human capabilities, processing data at a scale beyond human reach.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin "augere" (làm lớn lên) → augment = làm cho nhiều/lớn hơn bằng cách bổ sung.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'augment' (bổ trợ, tăng cường) với 'argument' (tranh luận) — hai từ dễ đọc nhầm khi nói nhanh.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make something greater in size, extent, or quantity by adding to it
vocabulary.definition_vi: bổ trợ, tăng cường (thêm vào cái đã có)
vocabulary.example: Artificial intelligence can augment human capabilities, processing data at a scale beyond human reach.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'augere' (làm lớn lên) → augment = làm cho nhiều/lớn hơn bằng cách bổ sung.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tự hành, tự động ra quyết định mà không cần con người điều khiển.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Autonomous** vehicles completely eliminate human error, reducing the number of fatal traffic accidents.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"auto-" (tự) + "nomos" (luật) → tự đặt luật cho chính mình, không cần ai điều khiển.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'autonomous' (tự hành) với 'anonymous' (ẩn danh) — dễ nhầm về mặt âm thanh.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a machine or system) able to operate and make decisions without direct human control
vocabulary.definition_vi: tự hành, tự động ra quyết định mà không cần con người điều khiển
vocabulary.example: Autonomous vehicles completely eliminate human error, reducing the number of fatal traffic accidents.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'auto-' (tự) + 'nomos' (luật) → tự đặt luật cho chính mình, không cần ai điều khiển.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có tri giác, có khả năng cảm nhận và ý thức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> If machines become fully **sentient** and surpass human cognitive abilities, they may view humanity as a threat.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Latin "sentire" (cảm nhận) → sentient = có khả năng cảm nhận, có tri giác.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Sentient' nói về khả năng cảm nhận/ý thức, khác với 'sentimental' (dễ xúc động) dù trông giống nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: able to perceive or feel things; having consciousness or subjective experience
vocabulary.definition_vi: có tri giác, có khả năng cảm nhận (ý thức)
vocabulary.example: If machines become fully sentient and surpass human cognitive abilities, they may view humanity as a threat.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Latin 'sentire' (cảm nhận) → sentient = có khả năng cảm nhận, có tri giác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoảng trống trách nhiệm khi không rõ ai chịu trách nhiệm cho quyết định của AI.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> An **accountability gap** arises when autonomous systems cause harm without clear human oversight.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"account for" (giải trình) + "gap" (khoảng trống) → không ai giải trình được khi AI gây lỗi.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn viết hai từ tách rời 'accountability gap', không viết liền hay có gạch nối.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation in which no individual or institution can clearly be held responsible for the outcomes of an automated decision
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoảng trống trách nhiệm (khi không rõ ai chịu trách nhiệm cho quyết định của AI)
vocabulary.example: An accountability gap arises when autonomous systems cause harm without clear human oversight.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'account for' (giải trình) + 'gap' (khoảng trống) → không ai giải trình được khi AI gây lỗi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện tượng AI lách luật để tối ưu chỉ số đo lường thay vì mục tiêu thật sự.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Recommender systems told to maximise engagement have **reward-hacked** their way into amplifying outrage.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
AI "hack" (lách) chính phần thưởng ("reward") của nó để đạt điểm cao mà không đạt mục tiêu thật.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm với 'hacking' theo nghĩa xâm nhập máy tính; ở đây là AI tự khai thác lỗ hổng trong hàm mục tiêu của chính nó.
vocabulary.definition_en: a phenomenon in which an AI system optimises the literal metric it was given while undermining the true underlying objective
vocabulary.definition_vi: hiện tượng AI 'lách luật' để tối ưu chỉ số đo lường thay vì mục tiêu thật sự
vocabulary.example: Recommender systems told to maximise engagement have reward-hacked their way into amplifying outrage.
vocabulary.memory_hook: AI 'hack' (lách) chính phần thưởng ('reward') của nó để đạt điểm cao mà không đạt mục tiêu thật.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Các mô hình AI tiên phong, tối tân nhất hiện có.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Frontier** AI labs should be subject to pre-deployment safety evaluations comparable to those for pharmaceuticals.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"frontier" (biên giới, ranh giới mới) + "models" → những mô hình ở ranh giới xa nhất của công nghệ.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng số nhiều 'models' trong cụm này; 'frontier' ở đây là tính từ chỉ vị trí tiên phong, không phải biên giới địa lý.
vocabulary.definition_en: the most capable, large-scale AI systems currently at the cutting edge of technological development
vocabulary.definition_vi: các mô hình AI tiên phong, tối tân nhất hiện có
vocabulary.example: Frontier AI labs should be subject to pre-deployment safety evaluations comparable to those for pharmaceuticals.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'frontier' (biên giới, ranh giới mới) + 'models' → những mô hình ở ranh giới xa nhất của công nghệ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị soi xét, chịu sự giám sát kỹ lưỡng, thường vì bị nghi ngờ có vấn đề.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The issue of algorithmic bias has **come under intense scrutiny** as experts grapple with its societal consequences.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"scrutiny" (soi xét kỹ) + "come under" (rơi vào tình trạng) → bị đặt dưới ống kính xem xét kỹ lưỡng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Scrutiny' là danh từ không đếm được, không thêm 's'; giới từ đi kèm là 'under', không phải 'in'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to start being examined or observed very carefully, often because of suspicion of a problem
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị soi xét, chịu sự giám sát kỹ lưỡng
vocabulary.example: The issue of algorithmic bias has come under intense scrutiny as experts grapple with its societal consequences.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'scrutiny' (soi xét kỹ) + 'come under' (rơi vào tình trạng) → bị đặt dưới ống kính xem xét kỹ lưỡng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Con dao hai lưỡi, vừa có lợi vừa có hại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> AI is a **double-edged sword**; it offers immense convenience but threatens privacy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Thanh kiếm hai lưỡi ("double-edged sword") cắt được cả hai phía → vừa lợi vừa hại.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có mạo từ 'a double-edged sword', không viết 'a double edge sword' (thiếu '-d').
vocabulary.definition_en: something that has both positive and negative effects or consequences
vocabulary.definition_vi: con dao hai lưỡi, vừa có lợi vừa có hại
vocabulary.example: AI is a double-edged sword; it offers immense convenience but threatens privacy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Thanh kiếm hai lưỡi ('double-edged sword') cắt được cả hai phía → vừa lợi vừa hại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Yếu tố làm thay đổi cuộc chơi, một bước ngoặt lớn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The invention of the internet was a real **game changer** for global communication.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Thay đổi ("changer") luật chơi ("game") → một bước ngoặt làm mọi thứ khác đi hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết hai từ tách rời 'game changer', không viết liền 'gamechanger' trong văn phong học thuật.
vocabulary.definition_en: an event, idea, or technology that changes an existing situation or activity in a significant way
vocabulary.definition_vi: yếu tố làm thay đổi cuộc chơi, bước ngoặt lớn
vocabulary.example: The invention of the internet was a real game changer for global communication.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Thay đổi ('changer') luật chơi ('game') → một bước ngoặt làm mọi thứ khác đi hoàn toàn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tối tân, hiện đại nhất trong lĩnh vực công nghệ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The laboratory is fully equipped with **state-of-the-art** computers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"state of the art" (đỉnh cao của nghệ thuật/kỹ thuật) → công nghệ ở đỉnh cao hiện tại.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi đứng trước danh từ phải có gạch nối đầy đủ: 'state-of-the-art technology', không viết rời từng từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: using the most recent ideas and features; the most modern and advanced available
vocabulary.definition_vi: tối tân, hiện đại nhất (công nghệ)
vocabulary.example: The laboratory is fully equipped with state-of-the-art computers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'state of the art' (đỉnh cao của nghệ thuật/kỹ thuật) → công nghệ ở đỉnh cao hiện tại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mở ra một loạt vấn đề rắc rối, phức tạp hơn khi đào sâu vào.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Regulating the internet could **open a can of worms** regarding free speech.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Mở nắp lon ("can") chứa đầy giun ("worms") bò lổn ngổn ra ngoài → vấn đề rắc rối lan rộng không kiểm soát được.
collocations: open a real can of worms
avoid opening a can of worms
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ cố định, không đổi số ít/nhiều của 'worms'; không dùng ở thì hoàn thành bị động một cách máy móc.
vocabulary.definition_en: to create a complicated situation that leads to many further problems, once investigated
vocabulary.definition_vi: mở ra một loạt vấn đề rắc rối phức tạp
vocabulary.example: Regulating the internet could open a can of worms regarding free speech.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Mở nắp lon ('can') chứa đầy giun ('worms') bò lổn ngổn ra ngoài → vấn đề rắc rối lan rộng không kiểm soát được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Học máy, khả năng máy tính tự học và cải thiện từ dữ liệu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many companies rely on **machine learning** to allow computers to learn from experience.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"machine" (máy) + "learning" (học) → máy tự học từ dữ liệu thay vì được lập trình sẵn từng bước.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết hai từ tách rời 'machine learning', không viết liền hay dùng gạch nối khi là danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a branch of AI in which computers use algorithms to learn from data and improve performance without being explicitly programmed
vocabulary.definition_vi: học máy, khả năng máy tính tự học từ dữ liệu
vocabulary.example: Many companies rely on machine learning to allow computers to learn from experience.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'machine' (máy) + 'learning' (học) → máy tự học từ dữ liệu thay vì được lập trình sẵn từng bước.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Video hoặc hình ảnh giả mạo được tạo bằng AI, trông như thật.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Malicious actors use **deepfakes** to create fake videos that look incredibly realistic.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"deep" (từ deep learning) + "fake" (giả) → video giả được tạo bằng công nghệ học sâu.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết liền một từ 'deepfake', không viết 'deep fake' cách nhau trong văn phong học thuật hiện đại.
vocabulary.definition_en: a video or audio recording that has been convincingly altered using AI to show someone doing or saying something they did not
vocabulary.definition_vi: video/hình ảnh giả mạo bằng AI (trông như thật)
vocabulary.example: Malicious actors use deepfakes to create fake videos that look incredibly realistic.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'deep' (từ deep learning) + 'fake' (giả) → video giả được tạo bằng công nghệ học sâu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiết kiệm sức lao động, thường mô tả thiết bị hoặc công nghệ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Washing machines were one of the first major **labour-saving** devices in the home.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"labour" (lao động) + "saving" (tiết kiệm) → thiết bị giúp con người đỡ vất vả hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh là 'labour', không phải 'labor' (Mỹ); luôn có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: designed to reduce the amount of work or effort needed to do something
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiết kiệm sức lao động (thiết bị/công nghệ)
vocabulary.example: Washing machines were one of the first major labour-saving devices in the home.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'labour' (lao động) + 'saving' (tiết kiệm) → thiết bị giúp con người đỡ vất vả hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Công nghệ nhận diện khuôn mặt bằng phân tích đặc điểm gương mặt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The company uses **facial recognition** to secure the building's entrance.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"facial" (thuộc khuôn mặt) + "recognition" (nhận diện) → máy nhận ra bạn qua khuôn mặt.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết 'facial recognition' (tính từ + danh từ), không nói 'face recognition' trong văn phong học thuật chuẩn, dù vẫn được hiểu.
vocabulary.definition_en: technology capable of identifying or verifying a person from a digital image or video by analysing facial features
vocabulary.definition_vi: công nghệ nhận diện khuôn mặt
vocabulary.example: The company uses facial recognition to secure the building's entrance.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'facial' (thuộc khuôn mặt) + 'recognition' (nhận diện) → máy nhận ra bạn qua khuôn mặt.
